'''''Alsophila dregei''''', [[Synonym (taxonomy)|synonym]] '''''Cyathea dregei''''',<ref name=CFLW/> ('''common tree fern''' or '''''gewone boomvaring''''' in [[Afrikaans]]) is a widespread species of [[Cyatheales|tree fern]] in [[southern Africa]].<ref name=LargBrag04/>

Within [[South Africa]], it co-occurs with the indigenous [[Gymnosphaera capensis|forest tree fern]] (''Gymnosphaera capensis'') and the invasive ''[[Sphaeropteris cooperi]]'' from [[Australia]]. Further north, outside of South Africa, it coexists with an additional two tree fern species, ''[[Alsophila manniana|A. manniana]]'' and ''[[Alsophila thomsonii|A. thomsonii]]''.<ref name=LargBrag04/>

This species is locally known as the common South African tree fern or grassland tree fern (in contrast to its relative, the [[Gymnosphaera capensis|forest tree fern]]). It is commonly known as the ''gewone boomvaring'' in [[Afrikaans]].

==Description==
===Key characteristics===
[[File:Cyathea dregei, pinna, Iphithi NR.jpg|thumb|right|The smallest leaflets have distinctively smooth (entire) margins]]
''Alsophila dregei'' has an erect, stout trunk and is up to {{convert|5|m|ft}} tall and 20–45 cm in diameter. It is a variable species, usually having a thick trunk and dense crown.  It is occasionally branched. [[Frond]]s are [[tripinnate]] (rarely [[bipinnate]]) and may reach 3 m in length. They are characteristically large and arching, with the lowest [[pinnation|pinnae]] usually reduced. The upper surface of fronds is glabrate, while the lower surface may be tomentose. The [[rachis]] and [[Stipe (botany)|stipe]] are brown in colouration and have a rough surface. The stipe is covered in brown [[scale (zoology)|scale]]s. Up to twelve [[sorus|sori]] occur per group per [[pinnule]].<ref name=LargBrag04/>

===Comparison to other tree ferns===

It can be distinguished from the [[Gymnosphaera capensis|forest tree fern]] (''Gymnosphaera capensis'') by its thick trunk, and by its smallest (third level) leaflets. The leaflets of ''A. dregei'' have smooth (entire) margins, while those of ''G. capensis'' are serrated. Each leaflet of ''A. dregei'' has multiple [[Sorus|seedcases]] on its underside, while a leaflet of ''G. capensis'' has only one per leaflet. The [[frond]]s of ''A. capensis'' come off lower, and it usually has several small, residual leaf remnants, which sprout in tufts among its fronds at the top of its stem.<ref>{{Cite web | last1=Latti | first1=Ivan | url=https://www.operationwildflower.org.za/index.php/albums/ferns/cyathea-dregei-il-2-1892 | title=Alsophila dregei | work=Operation Wildflower }}</ref><ref>Burrows, J.E. (1990) ''Southern African Ferns and Fern Allies''. Frandsen, Sandton. p.86.</ref><ref>[http://fernsofafrica.com/blank-species.php?species_id=101240 Ferns of Africa - ''Cyathea dregei'']</ref><ref>Thomas, V. (2002) ''Sappi Tree Spotting: Highveld and the Drakensberg: Tree & Shrub Identification Made Easy'' Jacana Media, p.52.</ref>

The only other indigenous tree ferns of the southern African region, ''[[Alsophila manniana]]'' and ''[[Alsophila thomsonii|A. thomsonii]]'', are both native to [[Zimbabwe]]. They can be distinguished from ''A. dregei'' by stem, stalk and frond appearance. ''A. manniana'' has sharp spikes on a slender trunk and frond stems. ''A. thomsonii'' has light-coloured, twisted hairs under its leaflets.<ref>{{Cite web | last1=Latti | first1=Ivan | url=https://www.operationwildflower.org.za/index.php/albums/ferns/cyathea-dregei-il-4-5488 | title=Alsophila dregei frond | work=Operation Wildflower }}</ref>

The invasive ''Sphaeropteris cooperi'' can be distinguished from ''A. dregei'' by the hairy white and brown scales on the new unfurling leaf stipes and sometimes by faint serrations on the leaflets.{{cn|date=March 2023}}

==Taxonomy==

The specific [[epithet]] ''dregei'' commemorates [[Johann Franz Drège]] (1794–1881), a [[Germany|German]] plant collector and explorer who worked extensively in South Africa and who is referred to as Drège when citing botanical names.<ref name=LargBrag04/>

==Distribution and habitat==
It is distributed widely in sub-Saharan Africa, including Guinea, Sierra Leone, Ghana, Nigeria, and Cameroon in west and west-central Africa, and in eastern and southern Africa from the Democratic Republic of the Congo and Uganda to South Africa. It is also native to [[Madagascar]]. In West Africa it grows in mountain and plateau grasslands and woodlands from {{convert|2500|–|7400|ft|m}} elevation.<ref>[https://powo.science.kew.org/taxon/urn:lsid:ipni.org:names:17532740-1 ''Alsophila dregei'' (Kunze) R.M.Tryon]. ''[[Plants of the World Online]]''. Retrieved 19 October 2023.</ref>

''Alsophila dregei'' grows on stream banks, in forest margins and in grasslands. It often grows in the open, in full, direct sunlight, provided there is sufficient moisture. Plants are most common at elevations of {{convert|900|-|1800|m|ft}}. In the wild, it is known to be fire resistant.{{cn|date=March 2023}}

==Cultivation==
''Alsophila dregei'' is rarely common in cultivation as an [[ornamental plant]], especially in South Africa and [[Australia]]. Plants should be sheltered and grown in rich [[humus]], with a constant supply of moisture. This species can survive light frosts with little damage.
